_doc: MOSES AND KIRKLAND, HISTORY OF CHICAGO, ILLINOIS, VOLUME I (1895) - THIRTY-FOUR CLAIMS OUT OF THE THREE PLACES IN 1,056 LEAVES WHERE THE VOLUME TOUCHES 1835. T-0581 came off the Newberry genealogical index (T-0570), which cites this work on 76 of its 581 Chicago and Cook County cards and points at 66 surnames this project already holds. THE READING IS IN THREE PARTS AND ONLY THE FIRST IS A CLOSE READ. bk_mk1_001 to bk_mk1_027 are Chapters V and VI - 'Rudimentary: the Log Cabin Age' and 'From Village to City, 1830 to 1837: the Balloon Age', leaves 89-141 - read line by line for the town before 1836. bk_mk1_028 to bk_mk1_033 are the two biographical sketches in the volume's back half of men who were IN the town before 1836: P. F. W. Peck and Philo Carpenter. bk_mk1_034 is the volume's own list of its biographies, which is what answers the ticket's actual question. THE OTHER 900 LEAVES WERE SWEPT BY SURNAME AND NOT READ, and coverage.json says so: they are Chicago after 1848 and the forty-odd lives of men who made their names in it. NOTHING IN data/residents/, data/households/, data/businesses/, data/structures/ OR data/assets/ WAS EDITED BY THIS PASS - the ticket routes every offer through the receiving layer's own PR, and this is the source pass.

claims.quote: Mr. Carpenter was the proprietor of the first drug store in the town; and George W. Dole and P. F. W. Peck erected the first frame buildings used for business purposes, the former on the southeast corner of South Water and Dearborn; and the latter on the southeast corner of South Water and La Salle streets.
claims.normalized: Philo Carpenter kept the town's first drug store; George W. Dole and P. F. W. Peck put up the first frame buildings used for business, Dole's on the south-east corner of South Water and Dearborn and Peck's on the south-east corner of South Water and La Salle.
claims.entities: Philo Carpenter; George W. Dole; P. F. W. Peck
claims.notes: A PLACEMENT ON TWO CORNERS THIS PROJECT MODELS, from a 1895 compilation and therefore a rung below the printed 1839 directory and the newspapers. Offered to the structures layer, NOT written into it here: the ticket routes a placement through that layer's own PR. Note the volume dates the pair to the 1832 paragraph and Andreas dates Dole's building to 1832 as well; the corner Peck is given here is the store corner, and the brick DWELLING of bk_mk1_031 is a different building on a different corner four years later.

claims.quote: Among these in 1832 were Philo Carpenter, and John S. Wright from Massachusetts; T. W. Goodrich, Hamilton Barnes, Dr. Philip Maxwell from New York; Dr. E. 8. Kimberly, George W. Snow, of Vermont, and Alanson Sweet.
claims.normalized: The volume's list of 1832 arrivals who stayed: Philo Carpenter and John S. Wright from Massachusetts; T. W. Goodrich, Hamilton Barnes and Dr. Philip Maxwell from New York; Dr. E. S. Kimberly and George W. Snow of Vermont; and Alanson Sweet.
claims.entities: Philo Carpenter; John S. Wright; T. W. Goodrich; Hamilton Barnes; Philip Maxwell; E. S. Kimberly; George W. Snow; Alanson Sweet
claims.notes: AN ARRIVAL-YEAR LIST, WHICH IS EVIDENCE OF PRESENCE AND NOT OF A HOUSEHOLD. It bears on the residents layer's arrival dates for Carpenter, Wright, Maxwell, Kimberly and Snow, all of whom this project already holds. Carpenter is one of the Newberry index's Moses-and-Kirkland lead surnames and this is the first of four places the volume carries him.

claims.quote: The first of these to be built was across the north branch for the use of foot passengers only, and was erected by Samuel Miller. One across the south branch, near Randolph street, at first consisted of floating logs tied together, but was subsequently recon- structed,was used until 1840. It was built by Alanson H. and Charles Taylor from funds raised by subscription,amounting to $486.20, of which the Indians of the vicinity con- tributed $200.
claims.normalized: The first bridge was a foot bridge over the north branch put up by Samuel Miller; the south-branch bridge near Randolph street began as floating logs tied together, was afterwards rebuilt and was used until 1840; it was built by Alanson H. and Charles Taylor out of a $486.20 subscription of which the neighbouring Indians gave $200.
claims.entities: Samuel Miller; Alanson H. Taylor; Charles Taylor
claims.notes: TWO CROSSINGS THE SCENE HAS TO DECIDE. The quote is cut at 'contrib' because the OCR runs the sentence on; the $200 figure is in the same line and is read in the normalized reading, not quoted. Offered to the structures layer rather than written into it.

claims.quote: The year 1832 also witnessed the beginning of the slaughtering and packing business of Chicago by George W. Dole, A. Clybourn, the Noble brothers, and Gurdon S. Hubbard
claims.normalized: Chicago's slaughtering and packing trade began in 1832 with George W. Dole, Archibald Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard.
claims.entities: George W. Dole; A. Clybourn; the Noble brothers; Gurdon S. Hubbard
claims.notes: HUBBARD IS A LEAD SURNAME and this project already holds him and his warehouse. The claim adds a trade and a year, not a place.

claims.quote:
John $. C. Hogan was appointed postmaster Novem- ber 2, 1832, and received and distributed mail in a room partitioned off for that pur- pose from his story-and-a-half storehouse, a
log building 45x18, situated at the angle formed by the intersection of Lake and South Water streets.
claims.normalized: John S. C. Hogan was appointed postmaster 2 November 1832 and kept the mail in a room partitioned off from his storey-and-a-half storehouse, a log building 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet.
claims.entities: John S. C. Hogan
claims.notes: A DIMENSIONED LOG BUILDING ON A NAMED ANGLE. 45x18 feet is a measurement the structures layer can use if it accepts a 1895 compilation for one; it is offered, not adopted.

claims.entities: John Dean Caton; John K. Botsford; Silas B. Cobb; Charles Cleaver; Walter Kimball; H. W. Knickerbocker; Ezekiel Morrison; Asahel Pierce; Hibbard Porter; Stephen Rexford; Henry Whitehead; Eli B. Williams; John T. Temple; Jeremiah Porter; Allan B. Freeman
claims.notes: THREE LEAD SURNAMES AT ONCE - caton, kimball and pierce - and all three are people this project already holds. The list is an arrival year and nothing more; it places nobody.

claims.quote: The fact that a comparatively large num- ber of frame buildings was erected this year (1833) —abont 165—indicates a corresponding influx of permanent settlers. They nearly all located on either South or North Water streets. One brick building was also erected—the first in the town outside the fort. It was built by Alanson Sweet and Wm. Worthingham, for John Noble, on a lot adjoining that afterwards oceupied by the Lake House, on the North Side.
claims.normalized: About 165 frame buildings went up in 1833, nearly all of them on South or North Water street, and one brick building - the first in the town outside the fort - was built by Alanson Sweet and William Worthingham for John Noble on a lot next to the one the Lake House afterwards took, on the North Side.
claims.entities: Alanson Sweet; William Worthingham; John Noble
claims.notes: THE FIRST-BRICK-BUILDING SENTENCE, AND THE VOLUME CONTRADICTS ITSELF ABOUT IT. Here the first brick building outside the fort is John Noble's, in 1833; at bk_mk1_022 the biographical section calls P. F. W. Peck's 1836 dwelling 'the first structure of that material put up in the town'. Both are printed in the same volume and this project does not resolve them here - see the source record's what_it_does_not_supply.

This was decided upon

claims.normalized: The town's incorporation was decided at a public meeting on 5 August 1833, at which only thirteen of the twenty-eight legal electors voted - twelve for, and Russel E. Heacock alone against.

claims.notes: A NAMED ROLL OF THE TOWN'S ELECTORS TWO YEARS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE, and this project already holds most of it. 'William Ninson' is the OCR's reading of what other printings give as William Nelson and is quoted as printed. Philo Carpenter is the only Moses-and-Kirkland lead surname on the roll. The volume adds that Heacock's name is absent because he lived outside the town limits, and that the former French and Indian voters are absent altogether.

claims.quote: Dole was appointed treasurer September 3d, and the first business transacted was the licensing of another free ferry across the river at Dearborn street. with Charles H. Chapman asferryman. November 7th Ben- jamin Jones was appointed street commis- sioner and Isaac Harmon town collector. December 4th George W. Snow was ap- pointed assessor and surveyor, and J. D. Caton corporation attorney.
claims.normalized: George W. Dole was made town treasurer on 3 September 1833; the board's first act was to license a free ferry at Dearborn street with Charles H. Chapman as ferryman; Benjamin Jones became street commissioner and Isaac Harmon town collector on 7 November; George W. Snow assessor and surveyor and J. D. Caton corporation attorney on 4 December.
claims.entities: George W. Dole; Charles H. Chapman; Benjamin Jones; Isaac Harmon; George W. Snow; J. D. Caton
claims.notes: TWO LEAD SURNAMES IN OFFICE - jones and caton. A ferry at Dearborn street in 1833 is also a crossing the scene must decide against the 1834 drawbridge of bk_mk1_020.

claims.quote: November 6th the limits of the town were extended so as to embrace the territory be- tween what was subsequently known as Jack- son street on the south, Jefferson street on the west, Ohio street on the north, and State street on the east.
claims.normalized: On 6 November 1833 the town limits were extended to run from Jackson street on the south, Jefferson street on the west, Ohio street on the north and State street on the east.
claims.notes: THE 1833 BOUNDARY, superseded by the act of 11 February 1835 at bk_mk1_024. Both are offered to whatever holds the town's extent; neither is written into it here.

It touches four open tickets and none of them is decided here: 'Newberry and Dole' without a forename (T-0396), 'Matthias Mason' where the newspapers read 'Matthias Nason' (T-0407), 'P. claims.quote: The first brickyard was established by Tyler K. Blodgett, this year, and also the manufacturing establishment of Asahel Pierce.
claims.normalized: The town's first brickyard was set up by Tyler K. Blodgett in 1833, and Asahel Pierce's manufacturing establishment in the same year.
claims.entities: Tyler K. Blodgett; Asahel Pierce
claims.notes: TWO LEAD SURNAMES - blodgett and pierce - and the reason the Newberry index pointed at this work for them. A brickyard in 1833 is also the local supply the nine brick buildings of 1835 (bk_mk1_023) would have drawn on.

claims.quote: second story of the Baptist church, a frame building on the corner of South Water and Franklin streets, was used for the school room, having been arranged for that purpose.
claims.normalized: Granville T. Sproat's school of 1833 was kept in the second storey of the Baptist church, a frame building on the corner of South Water and Franklin streets, fitted up for the purpose.
claims.entities: Granville T. Sproat
claims.notes: A PLACEMENT FOR THE FIRST BAPTIST MEETING HOUSE - South Water and Franklin - which the same volume calls the 'Temple Building' at leaf 124. Offered to the structures layer.

claims.quote: The public improvementa of the town at this time consisted of an estray pen, built by Samuel Miller under contract for the county, costing $12, and a jail, constructed “оѓ logs well bolted together," located at the north- west corner of the public square.
claims.normalized: The town's public works in 1833 were an estray pen built by Samuel Miller under county contract for $12, and a jail 'of logs well bolted together' at the north-west corner of the public square.
claims.entities: Samuel Miller
claims.notes: THE JAIL'S CORNER IS NAMED and the public square is ground this project models. 'estray pen' and 'improvementa' are the OCR as printed.

claims.quote: The upstart village lies principally on the right bank of the river, above the fort. Nextin rank to the officers and commissioners may be noted certain storekeepers and merchants resident here, looking either to the influx of new set- tlers establishing themselvesin the neighbor- hood, or those passing yet farther to the westward, for custom and profit. Add to these a doctor or two, two or three lawyers, a land agent and five or six hotel keepers. These may be considered as stationary, and proprietors of the half a hundred clapboard houses around town.
claims.normalized: Latrobe, visiting in September 1833, put the village mainly on the right bank of the river above the fort, and reckoned its stationary people - storekeepers and merchants, a doctor or two, two or three lawyers, a land agent and five or six hotel keepers - the proprietors of about fifty clapboard houses.
claims.entities: Charles J. Latrobe
claims.notes: A BUILDING COUNT FOR SEPTEMBER 1833, at second hand: Moses and Kirkland are quoting Latrobe's The Rambler in North America, which this project can and should read directly rather than through this compilation. Recorded because the count brackets the 1835 town from below.

claims.quote: Thestreets of the village (in the fall) soon became deluged with mud. It lay in many places half a leg deep, up to the hubs of the carts and wagons in the middle of the streets, and the only sidewalk we had was a single plank stretched from one building to another.
claims.normalized: In the autumn of 1833 the village streets were mud half a leg deep, up to the hubs of carts and wagons in the middle of the street, and the only sidewalk was a single plank stretched from one building to another.
claims.entities: Granville T. Sproat
claims.notes: THE SURFACE OF THE STREET IN THE SEASON THE SCENE IS SET NEAR, from the schoolmaster who walked it - but printed in 1887, fifty-four years after, and quoted here from a 1895 compilation. It is a description and NOT a grade: data/datum.json is derived from committed ground control and nothing here touches it.

claims.quote: There was but one road from the town to the lake, which was laid out by the surveyor, forty feet wide from the east end of Water street through the reservation.
claims.normalized: In 1833 one road ran from the town to the lake, laid out by the surveyor forty feet wide from the east end of Water street through the reservation.
claims.notes: A WIDTH AND A COURSE for the only road across the Fort Dearborn reservation. Offered to the streets layer; the reservation's own geometry in this project comes from the plats and is not touched here.

claims.normalized: The first drawbridge, over the river at Dearborn street, was built in 1834 by the contractor Nelson R. Norton: 300 feet long, sixteen wide, with a double draw.

claims.quote: result of the State census taken this year between September 1st and De- cember showed that the population of Chicago numbered 3,297 and, as further evidence ofits progress,demonstrated the fact that there were forty-four stores (dry goods, hardware, and groceries), two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewelers, two tin and copper manufac- tories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physi- cians, and a lyceum and reading room. Of the buildings erected nine were of brick.
claims.normalized: The State census of 1835, taken between 1 September and December, gave Chicago 3,297 people, and with it a count of the town's trades: forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room; nine of the year's new buildings were brick.
claims.notes: THE MOST USEFUL FIGURE IN THE VOLUME FOR THIS PROJECT, AND IT IS TWO MONTHS AFTER THE SCENE DATE. The census was taken from 1 September 1835 and the scene is 1 July 1835, so 3,297 is a CEILING for the scene date and not a count of it; the trade tally is likewise an autumn tally. It is the kind of number that gets mis-cited as 'the 1835 population', and it is recorded here with its own date attached so that it cannot be. Offered to no layer: it is a check on the town's total, not a placement.

claims.quote: The limits of the town had been increased by act of the legislature of February 11, 1835, to include therein all the land east of State street from Twelfth street to Chi- cago avenue, except the Fort Dearborn reservation.
claims.normalized: An act of 11 February 1835 enlarged the town to take in all the land east of State street from Twelfth street to Chicago avenue, except the Fort Dearborn reservation.
claims.notes: THE TOWN'S LEGAL EXTENT ON THE SCENE DATE, five months before it. Supersedes bk_mk1_012.

Further evidence of progress was indicated bythe organization, in October, of the first
First Fire POOK and ladder fire company, Company. which appropriately adopted the cognomen of the “Pioneer.”
claims.normalized: The town's first hook and ladder company, the Pioneer, was organized in October 1835; a second followed and the two made a volunteer fire department.
claims.notes: THREE MONTHS AFTER THE SCENE DATE, so the scene has no fire company. Recorded because the biographical sketch at bk_mk1_030 dates the same company to 20 October 1835 and names P. F. W. Peck on its roll, and the two readings agree.

claims.quote: They also selected two pieces of ground which they ordered the surveyor to lay out as cemeteries. One of these comprised sixteen acres on the south side, near the corner of Wabash avenue and Twenty-third street, and the other twelve acres, on the north side, near Chicago avenue on Clark street. These were the first places set apart for the burial of the dead; there having hitherto been no special loca- tion,private grounds around the residence of the deceased being frequently used for that purpose.
claims.normalized: The 1835 trustees laid out the town's first two burial grounds - sixteen acres on the south side near Wabash avenue and Twenty-third street, and twelve acres on the north side near Chicago avenue on Clark street - there having been no set place before, private ground round the dead person's house being often used.
claims.notes: BEFORE 1835 THE TOWN BURIED ITS DEAD IN ITS OWN YARDS, which is a statement about the scene's ground and not only about its calendar. The two cemeteries are outside the modelled extent; the practice they replaced is inside it. Offered to nothing - it is a note for whoever furnishes the town.

claims.quote:
While he was not the first inhabitant or the oldest resident of Chicago, Mr, P. F.W. Peck was the first genaine immigrant who made a permanent settlement in what be- | came, during his lifetime, the great inland metropolis of the country. His arrival here: was in the summer of 1830. Previous to that time Fort Dearborn had been intermit- tently occupied by soldiers and agents of the United States, and about its wooden pali- sades had gathered a few families of French origin and mixed blood, occupied in trade with the wild Indian tribes. Only the au- tumn before the ‘‘ Town of Chicago” had
been marked out by surveyors on a section of canal land, but had no vestige of life, save the few hangers-on of the military post, and no habitations save their rude log cabins, and only two or three ofsuch. Chief among the primeval inhabitants were J. B. Beau- bien, and John and Robert A. Kinzie and their families. About the time of Mr. Peck’s arrival, at least during the same year, came T. J. V. Owen, G. Kercheval, John Miller and his brother Samuel. These constituted the leading residents of Chicago at the close of the year 1830.
claims.normalized: The sketch makes P. F. W. Peck the first genuine immigrant to settle permanently at Chicago, arriving in the summer of 1830, and names the leading residents at the close of that year: J. B. Beaubien, John and Robert A. Kinzie and their families, with T. J. V. Owen, G. Kercheval and John and Samuel Miller arriving about the same time.
claims.entities: P. F. W. Peck; J. B. Beaubien; John Kinzie; Robert A. Kinzie; T. J. V. Owen; G. Kercheval; John Miller; Samuel Miller
claims.notes: PECK IS ONE OF THE VOLUME'S FORTY-SEVEN BIOGRAPHIES and one of the Newberry index's lead surnames; this is the sketch the index points at. It is a 1895 obituary-grade life of a man who died in 1871, and its 1830 roll should be tested against the 1830 census this project already holds rather than adopted from it.

claims.quote: gathering logs from the sur- rounding prairie, he erected a small tene- ment in which he displayed his goods. 'Thus he opened a business which, pursued with unflagging resolution and active industry, was destined to bring him a fortune, and link his name with the commercial greatness of the wonderful metropolis of the West. The little log store was close to Fort Dear- born, but it was only a temporary location.
claims.normalized: Peck brought a stock of merchandise from New York by the Erie canal and the lakes and, gathering logs from the surrounding prairie, put up a small tenement to display his goods; the little log store stood close to Fort Dearborn and was only a temporary location.
claims.entities: P. F. W. Peck
claims.notes: A BUILDING AND A POSITION - 'close to Fort Dearborn' - and the position is too loose to place. It is recorded because the same man's later South Water and La Salle store (bk_mk1_001) and his 1836 brick dwelling (bk_mk1_031) are three different buildings that a surname-level reading would collapse into one.

claims.quote: His name was inscribed on the roll of the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company, which was or- ganized October 20th, 1835, and he was appointed Second Assistant Engineer of the infant Fire Department.
claims.normalized: Peck's name was on the roll of the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company, organized 20 October 1835, and he was made Second Assistant Engineer of the new fire department.
claims.entities: P. F. W. Peck
claims.notes: THE SAME COMPANY THE NARRATIVE DATES TO 'October' AT bk_mk1_026, HERE DATED TO THE DAY. The two readings are in one volume and they agree; 20 October 1835 is three and a half months after the scene date, so the scene has no fire company and no Peck on its roll.

claims.quote: The same year he was married to Miss Mary K. Wythe, a lady who had come to Chicago from Philadelphia, and the follow- ing year he erected at the southwest cor- ner of Washington and LaSalle streets a brick dwelling for a residence, the first struc- ture of that material put up in the town
claims.normalized: In 1836 Peck built a brick dwelling at the south-west corner of Washington and LaSalle streets, which the sketch calls the first brick structure put up in the town.
claims.entities: P. F. W. Peck
claims.notes: THE VOLUME CONTRADICTS ITSELF HERE AND THE CONTRADICTION IS THE POINT. bk_mk1_007 gives the first brick building outside the fort to John Noble in 1833, built by Sweet and Worthingham on the North Side; this sketch gives it to Peck in 1836. Both are printed in this volume. This pass does not resolve them and does not offer either to the structures layer as documented. WHAT IS USABLE IS THE DATE: Peck's brick house is 1836 and therefore is NOT standing on 1 July 1835.

claims.quote:
It was in the
month of July, 1832, and the place of land-
ing was the lake shore, opposite where the
Douglas monument now stands. From thence
they were transported to Fort Dearborn with
an ox team by Joe Ellis, who lived in a log
cabin near the place.
claims.normalized: Philo Carpenter landed at Chicago in July 1832, on the lake shore opposite where the Douglas monument stood in 1895, and was carried to Fort Dearborn by ox team by Joe Ellis, who lived in a log cabin near the place.
claims.entities: Philo Carpenter; Joe Ellis
claims.notes: AN ARRIVAL MONTH FOR A MAN THIS PROJECT HOLDS, and one more name - Joe Ellis, in a log cabin near the south lake shore - who is outside the modelled extent. The narrative at bk_mk1_002 gives Carpenter's arrival year only; this gives the month.

claims.quote: procuring the lease of a small log house standing near the river on the line of the future Lake street, opened his store of drugs, In the early winter he moved into better quarters, and the next summer built and occupied a store on what is now South Water street, between La Salle and Fifth avenue. Не added to his stock salt, sugar, hardware and other staple goods.
claims.normalized: Carpenter leased a small log house standing near the river on the line of the future Lake street and opened his drug store in it; in the early winter he moved to better quarters, and the next summer built and occupied a store on what became South Water street between La Salle and Fifth avenue, adding salt, sugar, hardware and other staple goods to his stock.
claims.entities: Philo Carpenter
claims.notes: THE STORE STANDING ON THE SCENE DATE IS THE THIRD OF THESE, built in the summer of 1833 on South Water between La Salle and Fifth avenue - and 'Fifth avenue' is the 1895 name of the street the 1830s called Wells. A block-level placement for the town's first druggist, offered to the structures layer and not written into it here.

claims.normalized: The second half of the volume's list of biographies, giving the page of each sketch: among them Jackson, Jones (Daniel Amasa, Fernando and William), Kimball (Mark), Peck (Philip F. W. and Ferdinand W.) and Raymond (Benjamin Wright).
claims.notes: THIS IS THE ANSWER TO THE TICKET'S QUESTION, IN THE VOLUME'S OWN WORDS. Of the sixty-six Moses-and-Kirkland lead surnames the Newberry index names, the volume carries a signed biography for eleven - Carpenter (three of them: Augustus A., Benjamin and Philo), Caton, Fullerton, Gray (portrait only), Garrett (portrait only), Jackson, Jones, Kimball, Peck and Raymond - and every one of those sketches is of a NINETEENTH-CENTURY CHICAGO FIGURE WHOSE LIFE THE VOLUME TAKES PAST 1870. Only Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Philip F. W. Peck were in the town before 1836 at all. The first half of the same list is at leaf 23 lines 153-176 and is not quoted twice.
